column2: One should satisfy the ancestors with barley, rice, sesame, black gram, wheat and chickpeas, with green gram, shyamaka millet and mustard liquid;
with wild rice, hasti-shyamaka and priyangu one should offer arghya; the wise should give prasatika with tulika at shraddha.
Mango, amrataka, bilva, pomegranate, citron, ancient amalaka, milk, coconut, parushaka,
orange, with dates, grapes, blue kapittha, patola, priyala, karkandhu and jujube,
vikankata, vatsaka, kastvaru and varaka: these kinds of fruit should be carefully given at shraddha.
Jaggery, sugar, fish-egg (rock sugar), phanita, murmura, cow's milk, curd, ghee and sesame oil should be given,
rock salt and sea salt, sarasa salt; he should offer pure perfumes, sandal, aloe and saffron;
kalashaka, tandulika, vastuka, radish, and wild greens too he should give, and these flowers:
jati, champaka, lodhra, mallika, banabarbari, vrinta, ashoka, atarusha, tulasi and tilaka,
pavanti, shataparna, gandhashephalika, kubjaka, tagara, mriga, wild ketaki,
yuthika and atimukta are suitable for shraddha, Brahmins; the kamala, kumuda, padma and pundarika with care,
indivara, kokanada and kahlara one should use; kushtha, mamsi, valaka, kukkuti, jatipattraka,
nalikosha, ushira, musta, granthiparni and sundari; they say these and the like are suitable perfumes.
Guggulu, sandal, shrivasa and aloe, incense suitable for ancestors, and rishi-guggulu.
He should avoid rajamasha, chickpeas, lentils, koradushaka, viprusha, markata and kodrava grains.
He should avoid buffalo, chamara, deer, sheep and single-hoofed animal products, women's, camel's and sheep's curd, milk and ghee.
Palm, varuna and kakola, bahupattra, arjuni fruit, jambira, red bilva and even sala fruit he should avoid.
Fish, boar and tortoise and especially cows are to be avoided; putika, musk, rocana and padma-chandana;
kaleyaka, ugragandha and turushka too he should avoid; palanka, kumari, kirata, pindamulaka,
grinjana, chukrika, chukra, varuma, chanapattrika, jiva, shatapushpa, nalika and gandhashukara,
halabhritya, mustard, onion and garlic he should avoid; manakanda, vishakanda, vajrakanda, gadasthika,
purushalva with pindalu he should avoid at shraddha; bottle gourd, bitter leaves, pumpkin, the three pungents,
brinjal, shivajata, hairy banyans, kaliya, raktavana, balaka and lakucha
are to be avoided at shraddha; likewise the vibhitaka fruit, aranala and shukta, shirna and stale food.
Strongly smelling things should not be given, nor kovidaraka and shigru, nor what is too sour, slimy, thin, or stale, best of Brahmins.
What has lost its flavour and what smells of liquor should not be given; asafoetida, strongly smelling phanisha, bhunimba, nimba, rajika,
kustumburu, kalinga-born, amlavetasa he should avoid; pomegranate, magadhi, nagara, ginger and tittidi;
amrataka, jivaka and tumburu he should use; rice-pudding, shalmali, green gram, sweet cakes and the like with devotion;
panaka and rasala and cow's milk he should offer; whatever is to be eaten, sweet and unctuous, Brahmins,
slightly sour and pungent things should be given at shraddha; what is too sour, too salty or exceedingly pungent
is food for Asuras here; therefore he should avoid it far away. What is sweet, unctuous and slightly pungent and sour,
and tasty is food of the gods; he should use it at shraddha. Goat meat, vartika, partridge and hare flesh,
meat of shivala, lava, and rajiva fish he should use at shraddha; vagrinasa, red shiva, iron with scales,
and simhatunda and rhinoceros are said to be used at shraddha; and as Manu said, rohita fish may be used.
It should be used in oblations and funeral offerings, and he should not omit it. Thus it was said by me, Brahmins, observed by Varaha:
one who eats what has been forbidden by me goes to the Raurava hell; and these are forbidden by Varaha, rich in austerity.
What is not to be eaten by the twice-born is not to be given even to ancestors: he should avoid rohita, boar, tortoise, iguana and swan,
chakravaka and madgu, scaleless fish, kurara, boneless things, vasahata and cocks,
kalavinka and peacocks, bharadvaja birds and sharngaka, mongoose, owls, cats, lopa and others hard to take,
tittibha, sardhajambuka, tigers, bears and hyenas: whoever eats these and other defiled things, the evil-minded,
is a doer of great sin and goes to the Raurava hell; the sinner who gives these despised meats to ancestors
will cast even his ancestors in heaven into hell. Kusumbha greens, jambira, shigru, kovidaraka,
oil-cake, viprusha, lentils, grinjana, hemp, kodrava, kokilaksha, chukra, kambukapadmaka,
chakora and hawk meat, round gourd, talini and the fruit of palm trees: by eating these one goes to hell.
Having given them to the ancestors, a man goes with them to the river of pus; therefore the wise should by all efforts not bring them.
What has been forbidden by Varaha himself for ancestors' sake, with regard — better, sages, to eat one's own flesh
than ever to take the forbidden with respect. Whether through ignorance or negligence, if these forbidden things have once, Brahmins,
been eaten, one should then perform expiation with fruit, roots, curd, milk, buttermilk, cow's urine and barley gruel,
for each, seven days, when ordinary food has been eaten with it. Thus when the forbidden has been done even once by the twice-born,
the body is to be purified, especially by Vishnu's devotees. One should avoid the forbidden substance as said, best of Brahmins.
Having gathered, then shraddha should be done according to one's ability. Having thus done shraddha by rule suited to one's means, a man pleases the world from Brahma down to a blade of grass.
If one's father is living and the two fathers of the father are dead, how should shraddha be done? Tell us this in detail.
To whom the father would give shraddha, to him the son himself should give; thus neither worldly nor Vedic dharma is lost.
Brahmin, for one whose father is dead and whose grandfather is alive, how should he do shraddha? You ought to tell this.

He should give a pinda to his father and feed his grandfather; and a pinda to the great-grandfather; this is the determination in the scriptures.
brahmapuran:220:209	Pinda is to be given to the dead, and the living one should be fed; there is no Sapindikarana and no Parvana is desired.
brahmapuran:220:210	The man who follows the conduct based on the Pitrimedha (funeral rites) increases quickly in life, wealth and sons; no doubt.
brahmapuran:220:211	One who recites this chapter on the Pitrimedha at times of shraddha — his ancestors eat that food for three yugas, Brahmins.
brahmapuran:220:212	Thus the Pitrimedha ritual has been told by me, remover of sin and increaser of merit; it should be heard by self-controlled men and recited at shraddhas.
Then he should lie with his head to the south; the east is Indra's; he should not lie in perfumed water, nor at dawn.
Bathing at an eclipse is best, except by day; he should not wipe his limbs with the edges of garments or by hand-held cloths.
He should not shake his hair nor wring out his garments, nor take an unguent; the wise man should never do so unbathed.
Nor should he wear red clothes, nor variegated or black; nor should he reverse his garments or ornaments.
Garments to be avoided: a torn cloth, one very worn, one fallen into insects or hair, one looked at by dogs,
licked by a dog, spoiled by removal of essence; he should avoid back-flesh, useless flesh and forbidden flesh.
A man should not eat salt directly always; he should avoid, Brahmins, what has been long kept, dry or stale.
Preparations of flour, vegetables, sugarcane and milk, best of Brahmins, and meat preparations are not to be avoided even if long kept.
He should avoid sleep at sunrise and sunset; a man should not sleep unbathed, nor while sitting, nor with distracted mind.
Nor should he be seated on the bed or ground making noise; he should never eat without giving to servants.
A man should eat when bathed, evening and morning, by rule. A wise man should not go to others' wives.
Going to another's wife destroys men's merit, wealth and life; there is nothing in the world so life-shortening
as a man's touching another's wife. He should properly rinse his mouth and perform rites for gods, fire and ancestors, and salute teachers,
likewise the act of eating, with water free of foam, sound and smell, clear, with respect.
He should rinse likewise facing east or north; not from water in a pond, from a dwelling, from anthills or from rat-holes,
and the remnants of cleansing; he should avoid these five kinds of earth. Having washed hands and feet and sprinkled himself, attentive,
knees inside (arms between knees), a man should rinse three or four times, wipe twice, and touch the openings and the head.
Having properly rinsed with water, pure, he should perform the rite. After sneezing, licking, wind, spitting and the like,
he should rinse the mouth; on touching, or looking at the sun if not touched; he should also touch the right ear.
This is according to means; in the absence of the former, the later; when the former is not available, the later is desired.
He should not grind the teeth together, nor strike his own body; he should avoid sleep, journeying, eating and Vedic study.
At twilight, and also intercourse and departure; at the afternoon he should perform libation to ancestors with faith.
He should wash his head, for god and ancestors rites; he should have his beard attended to facing east or north.
He should avoid a deformed maiden; he should marry a healthy girl of good family, one beyond the seventh on the father's side and the fifth on the mother's.
He should protect wives, avoid jealousy, and by day sleep and intercourse; always avoid acts that cause pain to others and harm to creatures.
A menstruating woman of all varnas is to be avoided for four nights; to avoid female birth, the fifth too is to be avoided.
Then he should go on the sixth night, among the eldest even nights; on even nights sons are born, on odd nights daughters.
Unrighteous persons at parva's beginning, eunuchs at twilight times; in shaving and on Rikta days the wise man should avoid.
Words of the untrained should never be listened to, nor should a higher seat be given to the not-higher with respect.
After shaving and at the end of intercourse, Brahmins, the wise man should bathe with his clothes on and visiting a cremation ground.
Of gods, Veda, twice-born, the good, the truthful, the great-souled, teachers, devoted wives, performers of Brahma-sacrifice and ascetics,
he should not speak calumny nor mockery, Brahmins. Dressed in white garments, adorned with white flowers,
he should always be in auspicious dress and not wear the inauspicious; the learned should not be with the arrogant, mad, foolish or untrained.
He should not make friendship with the ill-conducted, nor with those defiled in age or birth, nor with spendthrifts, nor with enemies,
nor with the incompetent, the censured, nor with companions of rogues, nor with the poor or the quarrelsome, nor other such low men.
He should rise with friends, initiated persons, kings, graduates and fathers-in-law according to his means and honour them when they come to the house.
According to means, Brahmins, those who have stayed from year to year, having properly honoured them in the house in order by place,
he should then worship in the fire and give oblations in order: the first to Brahma, then to the lord of creatures,
third to the household deities, another to Kashyapa; then to Anumati, then a great offering.
The rite which I told earlier in the procedure of daily order — then he should do Vaishvadeva; Brahmins, hear:
Distributing by places, separately for the deities, he should give three to Parjanya, Apas and Dharitri at the maniká jar.
To Vayu in each direction; to the directions, in order east and so on; to Brahma, Antariksha and Surya, in order;
to the Vishvedevas and to the Vishvabhutas, to Usha, to the lord of beings, he should give on the north, pure.
Saying "Svadha" and "Namah" to the ancestors on the south, doing it apasavya, to the north-west saying "This for the sick."
He should give water mixed with remnants of food by rule; then he should make salutation to gods and to Brahmins.
The line north of the thumb of the right hand is called the Brahma tirtha, for rinsing.
Between the forefinger and thumb is declared the ancestral tirtha; by it he should give water to the ancestors, except in Nandimukha.
At the finger tips is the divine one; by it is the procedure of divine rites. The tirtha at the base of the little finger is of Prajapati there.
Thus by these tirthas he should always do the procedure with ancestors, always doing his duties, never with another tirtha.
Rinsing is praised with the Brahma tirtha, always the ancestral with the ancestral, for the gods with the divine tirtha, the Prajapati one with the victorious.
The wise should do the pinda-water rite of Nandimukhas with the Prajapati tirtha and whatever belongs to Prajapati.
The wise should not bear water and fire at once; he should not stretch his feet toward teachers, gods, ancestors or Brahmins.

He should not point out a cow that is drinking; he should not drink water with a cupped hand; at all times of purification, or with teachers or small things, the wise should not delay, nor blow fire with the mouth.
Brahmins, one should not live where these four are absent: a lender, a physician, a Shrotriya and a river with water.
Where the king has conquered his servants, is mighty and devoted to dharma, there the wise should always dwell; how is there happiness under a bad king?
Where citizens are well united and always follow justice, where people are peaceful and not envious, living there brings the rise of happiness.
In whose kingdom the farmers are mostly not overproud and where all herbs are, there the wise should dwell.
Brahmins, one should not live where these three are always: a conquest-seeker, old enmity, and people in constant festival.
The wise should always live among those of good character and fellow-goers, where the king is unassailable and where the land gives crops.
Thus this has been told to you, Brahmins, by me, out of desire for your welfare. Next I shall tell the rules of eating and drinking.
Food that is stale, soaked in oil and kept long may be eaten; even without oil, preparations of wheat, barley and cow-products too.
Hare, tortoise, iguana, porcupine, fish and shalyaka are edible; but village boar and cock are to be avoided.
What is left from ancestors and gods and the like at shraddha, out of desire of Brahmins, sprinkled and for medicinal purposes: eating meat so is not wrong.
Of conch, stone, gold, silver, ropes and garments, likewise of greens, roots and fruits, and bamboo and leather,
jewels, cloth, coral and pearl, vessels and cups: cleansing by water is desired.
Likewise of stone things by water and rubbing with stone; of oily vessels, by hot water.
Of winnowing baskets, deer-skins, pestle and mortar, and joined clothes, by sprinkling, and of a heap likewise.
Of all barks, cleansing by water and earth is desired; and likewise of all woollen things and hair.
By paste of mustard or paste of sesame again is purification, for those which have been defiled.
Likewise for cotton things, purity is by water and ashes; for wood, tooth, bone and horn, purity is desired by scraping.
Again by firing for earthen vessels, impurity; alms are pure, the hand of an artisan, goods for sale, and a woman's mouth.
The knowledge of a road's arrival, refined by a body of servants; what was earlier praised, long past, many times intervened, light,
within plentiful, and the child, and the doings of the old; workshops, houses and halls; a woman's two breasts are pure.
Waters are pure, flowing, free of smell; the earth is purified by time, burning, sweeping and cattle-herds.
A house by plastering, scratching, sprinkling, sweeping and the like; when hair or insects have fallen into food, or it is smelled by a cow, or has flies,
earth, water and ashes should be put in the food for purification. For copper vessels, by sour water; tin and lead by water;
purity of bronze vessels by ashes and water, and by flooding of liquid; what is stained with impurity by earth and water and removing smell.
Of other things also he should remove colour and smell. Meat is pure that is killed by Chandalas and flesh-eaters;
oil and the like on a road; cow's milk, giving satisfaction, is pure. Dust, fire, the shadow of a horse or cow, rays, wind, earth,
drops, flies and the like are not defiled by contact with the defiled. The mouth of a goat or horse is pure, not that of a cow or calf.
Pure is the milk flowing from the mother; a bird in knocking down fruit; seat, bed, vehicle, river banks and grass
are purified by moon, sun, rays and wind, as with goods for sale. On passing along a road, in bathing, in acts of sneezing and drinking,
one should rinse according to rule; in putting on garments; by touches of those touched, in water or mud of a double road;
for things built of baked brick, purity is by exposure to wind. From much-damaged food, the first portion should be taken out and discarded.
He should sprinkle the rest, rinse with water and earth; one who eats bad food should fast three nights.
In ignorance, or knowing beforehand, for pacifying its fault, and not for a menstruating woman or one touched, or one who stays after delivery, the outcaste —
having touched them, one should bathe for purity; likewise a corpse-carrier. A Brahmin who touches a human bone with fat is purified by bathing;
if without fat, only by rinsing, touching a cow or looking at the sun. He should not cross over spittle and rubbings.
Leftovers, faeces, urine and foot-water from the house should be thrown outside. Without lifting five pindas of earth one should not bathe in another's water.
He should bathe in god-dug ponds, Ganga, lakes and rivers; the wise should never stay in gardens and the like at improper times.
He should not converse with those hated by the people, women without heroes (widows), those who censure gods, ancestors, good scripture, sacrificers and renunciants.
